episodes.title: The End of Evangelion
episodes.subtitle: Theatrical alternate ending to episodes 25–26

entries.title: Shinji Ikari
entries.body: Gendo and Yui's son, summoned to Tokyo-3 by the father who abandoned him and put in the cockpit of Unit-01 the day he arrives. Withdrawn and conflict-averse, his search for a reason to exist beyond "the boy his father needs" is the show's emotional spine.

entries.scene: Wheeled in on a stretcher, too injured to pilot
entries.title: Rei Ayanami
entries.body: A quiet, compliant pilot grown rather than born — cloned from Yui Ikari's remains using the Angel Lilith's genetic material. Multiple physical copies of her exist in Terminal Dogma; the show is coy about how much continuity of self survives between them.

links.label: Where the clones live
Are the Reis the same person?

entries.title: Misato Katsuragi
entries.body: Commands Eva deployment in the field and takes Shinji in as a housemate. A Second Impact survivor whose father died in the disaster that created it, which shapes both her drive to fight the Angels and her difficulty staying close to anyone.

links.label: The disaster that shaped her

entries.title: Gendo Ikari
entries.body: Runs NERV and, through it, humanity's entire Angel defense as cover for a private goal: using the Human Instrumentality Project to reunite with his dead wife Yui, whose soul he believes persists inside Unit-01. Treats nearly everyone, including Shinji, as an instrument toward that end.

links.label: What he's actually building toward
How sympathetic is that, really?

entries.title: Ritsuko Akagi
entries.body: Oversees the Evangelions and the MAGI supercomputers, inheriting both her position and a tangled personal history from her mother, Naoko Akagi, the MAGI's original designer.

links.label: The system she inherited

entries.title: Second Impact (September 13, 2000)
entries.body: A catastrophic explosion at an Antarctic research site, publicly blamed on a meteorite. It melted the polar ice caps, shifted the Earth's axis, and killed roughly half the world's population. Later revealed as the result of a deliberate contact experiment on the being called Adam. One knock-on effect stated directly in the Japanese Wikipedia entry: the axis tilt erased Japan's seasons entirely, leaving the country in permanent summer-like weather for the rest of the series.

links.label: What was actually experimented on

entries.title: Tokyo-3 and the Angel War
entries.body: Fifteen years after Second Impact, the fortified city of Tokyo-3 is built over NERV's geofront headquarters specifically to fight the Angels, whose periodic attacks make up the bulk of the series' episodic structure. Mapped onto real-world geography, Tokyo-3 sits on the north shore of Lake Ashi, in Hakone, Kanagawa Prefecture — nowhere near the real Tokyo.

entries.title: NERV
entries.body: A UN-supervised paramilitary organization, publicly tasked with defending humanity from the Angels using the Evangelions. It answers, less publicly, to SEELE and to Gendo Ikari's own agenda.

links.label: Who NERV really answers to

entries.title: Angels (Shito)
entries.body: The beings NERV exists to fight, each biologically and tactically distinct, sharing an AT Field and a strong drive to reach Lilith in Terminal Dogma. Their exact origin and nature is never pinned down on-screen.

links.label: What are they, really?

entries.title: AT Field
entries.body: "Absolute Terror Field": a barrier every Angel and Evangelion projects, physically blocking conventional weapons. Late in the series it's reframed less as a shield and more as the boundary that keeps one soul separate from every other.

links.label: The plan to dissolve it entirely

entries.title: Evangelions
entries.body: Giant bio-mechanical units, piloted via synchronization with a teenage pilot's nervous system, built as humanity's only weapon capable of matching an Angel's AT Field. Their organic, unwilling-looking behavior under stress is a recurring source of unease.

links.label: The first sign they might be alive

entries.title: What are the Angels, biologically or metaphysically?
entries.body: "Offspring of Adam" is as precise as the show gets. Whether they're organisms, weapons, something closer to concepts, or all three depending on continuity is never fixed — and the Rebuild films decline to answer it too.

links.label: The Adam/Lilith mapping is shaky too

entries.title: Humanity is officially the 18th Angel
entries.body: NERV's own numbered Angel list (as reproduced on Japanese Wikipedia) runs Adam (1st) and Lilith (2nd) as the two progenitor Angels, Sachiel through Tabris/Kaworu as the 3rd through 17th, and then lists Lilin — humanity itself — as the 18th Angel. The show never dwells on this classification, but it quietly puts humans and the things they're fighting in the same taxonomic category.

links.label: The 3rd–17th Angels NERV actually fights

entries.title: Sailor Moon's fingerprints on the cast
entries.body: Several casting/naming choices trace back to Anno's fandom of Sailor Moon (which aired just before Eva): Misato's voice actress Kotono Mitsuishi was cast partly on the strength of her Usagi/Sailor Moon performance; Rei Ayanami's given name comes from Sailor Mars's civilian name, Hino Rei; and Kaworu Nagisa was modeled in part on Sailor Moon staffer Kunihiko Ikuhara, whom Anno was personally close with.

links.label: Misato
Rei
Kaworu

entries.title: Asuka Langley Souryuu
entries.body: A German-Japanese prodigy pilot whose relentless competitiveness is a defense mechanism built on childhood trauma (her mother's breakdown and suicide). Her arc tracks what happens when a self-worth built entirely on being needed as a pilot stops working.

entries.title: Ryoji Kaji
entries.body: Officially a NERV agent, unofficially reporting to SEELE and Japan's government simultaneously, digging into NERV's secrets — including Adam and Instrumentality — while romantically entangled with Misato.

links.label: The secret he keeps digging into
What that digging costs him

entries.title: Studio Ghibli animated this one
entries.body: Episode 11 — the MAGI-computer-meltdown, power-outage bottle episode — was farmed out to Studio Ghibli staff as a contracted production. It shows: the art style, character expressions, and tone come out noticeably more comedic and warm than the episodes around it.

entries.title: MAGI
entries.body: NERV's supercomputer system: three semi-independent processors — Casper, Melchior, and Balthasar, named for the Biblical Three Magi — modeled on different aspects of their designer Naoko Akagi's personality, which must reach consensus to authorize NERV's most critical decisions.

entries.scene: Episode title translates literally as "SEELE, Seat of the Soul"
entries.title: SEELE
entries.body: A secretive committee that founded NERV and steers events from behind it, working from the Dead Sea Scrolls toward its own version of the Human Instrumentality Project — a version Gendo Ikari is simultaneously trying to hijack for himself.

links.label: The text they're both working from

entries.title: What do the Dead Sea Scrolls actually say?
entries.body: SEELE and NERV both act on a text called the Dead Sea Scrolls that supposedly predicts the Angels' attacks and the path to Instrumentality. Its actual contents are never shown or quoted at length.

entries.title: The episode almost nobody saw live
entries.body: TV Tokyo bumped this episode to a New Year's Day 8:30am slot (instead of its normal Wednesday 6:30pm one) to make room for New Year's programming. The result was a 0.9% household rating — the lowest of the entire series, versus the finale's series-high 10.3%. Producers had anticipated the dip: a clip-show recap originally slotted for episode 14 was swapped with this episode instead, so the low-visibility slot fell on new content rather than a recap.

entries.scene: Power cable severed, plug depth critical — it keeps fighting anyway
entries.title: Unit-01's unpowered "berserk" state
entries.body: Unit-01 keeps fighting an Angel after its power cable is severed and its plug depth goes critical — something no dummy plug or external system explains. The show treats this as evidence the Eva itself is, in some sense, alive.

links.label: One reading of why
The forced-override system this isn't

entries.title: Yui's soul inside Unit-01
entries.body: The show never states in dialogue that Yui Ikari's soul resides in Unit-01, but strongly implies it — her disappearance during an activation test, Gendo's fixation on the unit, and Unit-01's unpowered "berserk" rescues of Shinji are the load-bearing evidence. Anno has confirmed the broader mechanism in interviews (a pilot syncs with an Evangelion "through their mother's soul," an idea he traces to an NHK documentary on the brain), which lends real weight to the reading — but the specific claim that it's Yui's soul in Unit-01 is still never said outright on-screen.

links.label: Where that ambiguity comes to a head

entries.scene: Gendo forces Unit-01 onto autopilot to destroy the Angel-possessed Unit-03
entries.title: The Dummy System (autonomous override)
entries.body: Distinct from the dummy plug used later in the mass-production Evas: this is an autonomous control system Gendo activates on Unit-01 itself, overriding Shinji's control entirely to destroy Unit-03 — which the 13th Angel has taken over — without Shinji's consent. Only afterward does Shinji learn his own friend, Toji Suzuhara, was in Unit-03's cockpit, maimed by his own Eva's hands. It's what finally makes Shinji quit piloting, right up until the next Angel attack forces his hand again.

links.label: The related but distinct mass-production system
Back to Shinji

entries.title: Dummy plug system
entries.body: An unmanned-operation system meant to let an Evangelion fight without a live pilot, built by transplanting a simulated version of a pilot's mental patterns into the entry plug — Rei's for Unit-00's dummy plug, and Kaworu's for the nine mass-production Evangelions (Units 05 through 13).

links.label: How much of a person is really in there
The related but distinct Unit-01 override

entries.title: Human Instrumentality Project
entries.body: The plan, pursued in incompatible versions by SEELE and by Gendo, to trigger a forced next stage of human evolution by dissolving every individual AT Field and merging all souls into one, via a ritual called the Third Impact.

links.label: The ritual that carries it out

entries.scene: Kaji lays out what the Katsuragi Expedition really did
entries.title: Adam
entries.body: The first of the beings created by the "First Ancestral Race" long before humanity; the Angels are described as Adam's offspring. A contact experiment on Adam is what triggered Second Impact.

links.label: Adam vs. Lilith, precisely which is which

entries.title: What was First Impact?
entries.body: Referenced as the event that shaped the Earth long before Second Impact, tied to Adam and Lilith's arrival. Different tie-in material describes it differently, and the TV series itself barely touches it.

entries.scene: Fuyutsuki is pressed on what Gendo is really after
entries.title: Gendo as tragic rather than purely villainous
entries.body: Gendo's plan is explicitly framed here as wanting to be with Yui again, but how much sympathy that deserves given the harm he causes Shinji and everyone around him to get there is a matter of ongoing viewer disagreement rather than something the text adjudicates for you.

links.label: Back to Gendo's introduction

entries.scene: Misato takes Shinji down into Terminal Dogma
entries.title: Lilith
entries.body: A being of the same origin as Adam, kept crucified and sealed in NERV's Terminal Dogma. The Lilin — i.e., humanity — are described as descended from Lilith rather than Adam, and Lilith's flesh and soul are the source material for the Evangelions and for Rei.

links.label: Her connection to Rei
Which of these two is which, again?

entries.title: Adam/Lilith identity mix-ups across versions
entries.body: Which being is sealed in Terminal Dogma, which one Gendo's faction actually possesses, and which one the embryo NERV keeps separately is called is inconsistent enough between the TV series, supplementary material, and later reprints that fans still debate the "correct" mapping. Some treat this as evidence of a deliberately unresolved cosmology rather than a continuity error.

entries.title: Kaji is killed
entries.body: Kaji is killed off-screen in this episode, having gotten too close to the truth about Adam, Lilith, and Instrumentality he'd spent the series digging into. Who specifically killed him (SEELE or Gendo's own faction) is left unstated.

links.label: Back to Kaji's introduction

entries.title: How much of a person is in a dummy plug
entries.body: The dummy plug is described as simulating a pilot's mental patterns rather than containing a true digitized soul, but the mass-production Evas' dummy plugs are built from Kaworu specifically, and their on-screen behavior (screaming, bleeding) reads as more than simulation. How much of that is meant literally is left to the viewer.

links.label: The Kaworu these are built from

entries.title: The Rei clones
entries.body: A tank of spare Rei bodies is kept in Terminal Dogma; when a given Rei dies, another takes her place, personality and memory carried over to a degree the show never fully explains.

links.label: Whether that's really "her"

entries.title: Lilith's soul divided across Rei and Unit-00
entries.body: Building on a scene in The End of Evangelion where Rei is welcomed "home" by Lilith, a popular theory holds that souls in this universe are divisible, and that a fragment of Lilith's soul persists in each Rei clone and possibly in Unit-00 itself (offered as one explanation for Unit-00's own unexplained hostile incidents). This is an inference from a handful of suggestive scenes, not a stated rule.

links.label: The scene this theory is built on

entries.title: Do the Rei clones share one continuous identity?
entries.body: Each Rei carries the prior one's memories to some extent, but the show never states whether that makes her the same person, a new person with inherited memories, or something in between — the question is posed to the audience more than once and never answered for them.

entries.title: Kaworu Nagisa
entries.body: Arrives late in the story as a new pilot candidate, forms an immediate bond with Shinji, and is then revealed to be an Angel in human form, sent by SEELE to reach Lilith in Terminal Dogma. Shinji is left to decide whether to kill him.

links.label: What he actually felt
Is he really an Angel, though?

entries.title: What Kaworu actually felt for Shinji
entries.body: Kaworu tells Shinji he loves him within a day of meeting him, then lets Shinji kill him rather than fight back. Whether this is genuine affection an Angel is nonetheless capable of, a calculated move to complete his mission, or both at once, is never resolved — the scene is written to support any of the three.

entries.title: Is Kaworu an Angel, in exactly the same sense the others are?
entries.body: Kaworu is called the Seventeenth Angel but presents as fully human and self-aware in a way none of the others do, and material outside the original TV run has described his origin differently. The TV series itself leaves the discrepancy alone.

entries.title: The title "最後のシ者" is a pun
entries.body: The Japanese title for this episode splits the kanji in Kaworu's surname, Nagisa (渚), into its component radicals and re-renders one as the katakana シ, so the title reads as "the last シ者" — deliberately ambiguous between 使者 ("messenger," SEELE's errand for Kaworu) and 死者 ("the dead," what he becomes by the end of it).

links.label: The Kaworu this refers to

entries.title: Acceptance vs. rejection of Instrumentality
entries.body: A common reading pairs the TV finale and The End of Evangelion as two sides of the same choice: the TV ending shows Shinji arriving at self-acceptance from inside a dissolved, unified consciousness, while EoE shows the same decision played out physically — Shinji ultimately rejecting total union with others in favor of a painful but individual existence. Neither film states this framing outright; it's inferred from how the two versions rhyme.

links.label: Why there are two endings at all
How EoE actually plays it out

entries.scene: The finale breaks into congratulatory character-actor cutaways
entries.title: The finale as commentary on Anno's own depression
entries.body: Director Hideaki Anno has spoken about depression during the show's production, and the TV finale's abrupt turn toward real-world footage, character-actor congratulations, and direct address to the viewer is widely read as breaking the fourth wall on purpose — a message about escapism versus engaging with a difficult reality, layered on top of Shinji's in-story arc rather than replacing it. Sociologist Miyadai Shinji has argued the series itself started as a lighter, more conventional "school anime" concept and drifted toward this ending as production wore on and the director's own state of mind changed. Anno's own framing, from a 1998 interview: he called the show closer to "a documentary" of himself than fiction, saying every character is a synthesis of his own personality, and that he simply doesn't have the ability to write drama that isn't a projection of himself.

entries.title: "I mustn't run away" becomes "it's okay to run away"
entries.body: Shinji's early refrain — "I mustn't run away" (逃げちゃダメだ) — is the closest thing the show has to a stated thesis in its first half. By the finale it's been replaced with the opposite: it's okay to run away. Character designer Yoshiyuki Sadamoto is credited with suggesting the shift.

links.label: How that plays out differently in EoE

entries.title: Why did the finale turn out this way? Even the staff disagree
entries.body: The standard explanation is that production had fallen catastrophically behind — only around a third of the episodes were fully animated by the time the show started airing, and the two finale episodes were assembled largely from recycled footage out of necessity. But several staff accounts complicate that: magazine editor Ogura Yuichiro says the finale's plot points were already locked in by January 1996, two months before broadcast; GAINAX president Yamaga Hiroyuki says the show was never so broken it couldn't have been finished conventionally; and assistant director Tsurumaki Kazuya has said Anno had "a chance of winning" with this ending in mind from the start, and considered the backlash itself part of that win — a show forgotten in six months was the actual failure state he was avoiding. Anno himself maintains the finale was always intended to be exactly this, schedule aside, aiming at what he called "liberation from cel animation."

links.label: The other ending this led to

entries.title: The original plan had 28 Angels, not 17
entries.body: Early planning documents describe 28 Angels rather than the 17 the finished show uses, with a climax involving a second wave of 12 Angels descending from the moon alongside Instrumentality's activation. That structural role — a large final wave of antagonists tied to Instrumentality — survives in the finished work in a different form: the nine Mass-Production Evangelions that SEELE deploys near the end.

links.label: The system built into those nine units
The plan they were meant to serve

entries.title: The wholly-new film that never got made
entries.body: The original 1996 plan was for both replacement final episodes to be an entirely new theatrical film, not a clip-show. Production fell too far behind again; at a February 1997 press conference — one month before the planned release — Anno publicly apologized, and the all-new film was scrapped. What released instead split into two films: a clip-show-plus-new-footage recap (Death (True)²) and then the genuinely new Air/まごころを、君に in July 1997. The original all-new concept became what Japanese sources call a "phantom project" (幻の企画) — never produced in that form.

links.label: Ideas from that scrapped draft
The ending that resulted instead

entries.title: Concepts from the scrapped all-new film
entries.body: Never filmed, so not part of any released continuity — but Anno has described draft ideas from the abandoned all-new film: pilots merging directly with an Evangelion's "womb" rather than using an entry plug, requiring a C-section-like extraction under a strict time limit (missing it meant the pilot's literal death), and Angels that prey on and consume people outright. Anno has noted the latter idea predates, and reads similarly to, Attack on Titan's premise by well over a decade.

links.label: Why this film was never made

entries.title: Two different endings exist
entries.body: The TV series' original episodes 25–26, made under a tightened budget, resolve the story almost entirely inside Shinji's own psyche. The End of Evangelion (1997), a theatrical film, was written and produced afterward as an alternate, effects-driven ending depicting Third Impact's events directly — both are considered canon, telling the same climax from different angles.

links.label: One way to read the pair together

entries.title: Third Impact
entries.body: The series' climax: the event that carries out (or nearly carries out) Human Instrumentality. What actually happens, and how much of it is undone by the end, differs between the TV series' final two episodes and the alternate ending in The End of Evangelion.

links.label: What's left afterward
Does it happen more than once?

entries.scene: Rei III dissolves into Lilith: "I'm home." / "Welcome home."
entries.title: Rei's reunion with Lilith
entries.body: In The End of Evangelion, Rei III is shown reuniting with Lilith with the words "I'm home," and Lilith replying "Welcome home" — one of the few moments the show gestures directly at what Rei actually is.

links.label: The soul-splitting theory this feeds

entries.scene: The final shot, on the beach
entries.title: What actually happens on the beach at the end of EoE
entries.body: The final shot — Shinji strangling, then stopping, Asuka, who touches his cheek and says "kimochi warui" ("disgusting" / "I feel sick") — is one of anime's most argued-over endings. Readings range from a literal moment between two survivors of a mostly-undone Third Impact, to a purely symbolic beat with no fixed literal status, to a bleak coda implying nothing is resolved. The film gives no voiceover or text to settle it.

links.label: What state the rest of the world is in

entries.title: A cyclical/recurring Third Impact
entries.body: Some fans read hints across the franchise (including the later Rebuild films, which explicitly restart the story after a Third Impact) as evidence that impacts recur in cycles rather than the original TV/EoE story being a one-off — though the original series itself makes no such claim; this reading leans heavily on later material re-interpreted backward.

entries.title: What state is the world actually in after The End of Evangelion?
entries.body: The final scene shows Shinji and Asuka alone on a wrecked shoreline. Whether this is a reversed, near-total, or partial Third Impact — and whether anyone else survived it — is left to the audience.
